title: Spartacus Slave Revolt

Spartacus a Thracian gladiator led the rebellion.
Army grew to 70,000 escaped slaves.
Defeated multiple Roman legions for two years.
Crucified 6,000 survivors along Appian Way.
Spartacus was a former gladiator who became the most feared rebel leader in Roman history.
The revolt threatened Rome's entire social order built on slavery.
Crassus and Pompey ultimately crushed the rebellion and claimed the glory.
His revolt began in 73 BC when, along with about 70 other gladiators, he escaped a gladiatorial school near Capua.
Although Spartacus is a significant figure in Roman history, no contemporary sources exist.
Little is known about him beyond the events of the war, and the extant accounts are contradictory.
All sources agree, however, that he was a former gladiator and accomplished military leader.

title: Cleopatra's Egypt
bullets: Last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt.
Spoke nine languages including Egyptian.
Allied with Julius Caesar then Mark Antony.
Died by snake bite or poison 30 BCE.
Her death ended 3,000 years of pharaonic rule.
Cleopatra was the last pharaoh of Egypt and a shrewd political strategist.
She aligned Egypt with Rome through relationships with Caesar and Mark Antony.
After her defeat, Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire.
Cleopatra began her reign alongside her brother Ptolemy XIII, but a falling-out between them led to a civil war.
A member of the Ptolemaic dynasty, she was a descendant of its founder Ptolemy I Soter, a Macedonian Greek general and companion of Alexander the Great.
Her first language was Koine Greek, and she is the only Ptolemaic ruler known to have learned the Egyptian language, among several others.
After her death, Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire, marking the end of the Hellenistic period in the Mediterranean.

title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
bullets: Crossed Alps in 218 BCE with war elephants.
Led Carthage against Rome in Second Punic War.
Crushed Romans at Battle of Cannae.
Wandered Italy 15 years without taking Rome.
Eventually defeated at Battle of Zama.
Hannibal's crossing of the Alps with war elephants remains one of history's boldest military maneuvers.
At Cannae he destroyed a Roman army nearly twice the size of his own.
Scipio Africanus finally defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE.
The Alps were not well-documented at the time.
The two primary sources for the event are Polybius and Livy, who were born c. 20 years and c. 160 years after the event, respectively.
Hannibal invaded Italy by crossing the Alps with North African war elephants.
Revanchism prevailed in Carthage, symbolized by the pledge that Hannibal made to his father to "never be a friend of Rome".

title: The Trojan War
bullets: Described in Homer's Iliad circa 8th century BCE.
Archaeological site of Troy found in modern Turkey.
Helen of Sparta sparked the legendary conflict.
Greeks used Trojan Horse trick to enter city.
Blurred line between myth and history for millennia.
Homer's Iliad and Odyssey immortalized the Trojan War for Western civilization.
Archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann excavated Troy in the 1870s.
The war symbolizes the blurred line between ancient myth and historical memory.
The war is one of the most important events in Greek mythology.
Other parts of the war are described in a cycle of epic poems, which have survived through fragments.
The Trojan War was a legendary conflict in Greek mythology that took place around the thirteenth or early twelfth century BC.
The war was waged by the Achaeans against the city of Troy after Paris of Troy took Helen from her husband Menelaus, king of Sparta.

title: Death of Socrates
bullets: Executed 399 BCE for corrupting Athenian youth.
Chose hemlock over exile.
Taught Plato who taught Aristotle.
His trial defined philosophy forever.
Socrates was charged with impiety and corrupting the youth of Athens.
He chose to drink hemlock rather than accept exile from his beloved city.
His student Plato preserved his teachings, shaping Western philosophy forever.
The death sentence of Socrates was the legal consequence of asking politico-philosophic questions of his students.
The Trial of Socrates was held to determine the philosopher's guilt of two charges against the city of Athens: asebeia and corruption of the youth.
The cause of death is usually considered important, and an autopsy can be done to determine it.
The study of death is known as thanatology. == Background == As of the early 21st century, 56 million people die per year.
Death of Socrates is usually dated to 399 BCE.

title: The Terracotta Army
bullets: Discovered 1974 by farmers digging a well.
Guards tomb of China's first emperor Qin Shi Huang.
Each figure has unique facial features.
Originally painted in bright colors.
Represents real army formations and weapons.
The terracotta warriors were buried to protect Qin Shi Huang in the afterlife.
An estimated 8,000 life-sized figures have been discovered so far.
The site near Xi'an remains one of the greatest archaeological finds of the 20th century.
The figures, dating from approximately the late 200s BCE were discovered in 1974 by local farmers in Lintong County, outside Xi'an, Shaanxi, China.
Estimates from 2007 were that the three pits containing the Terracotta Army hold more than 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots with 520 horses.
It is a form of funerary art buried with the emperor in 210–209 BCE in his mausoleum with the purpose of protecting him in his afterlife.
The Terracotta Army is a collection of terracotta sculptures depicting the armies of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China.

title: Great Wall of China
bullets: Construction began over 2,000 years ago.
Not one wall but many sections and dynasties.
Built to repel northern nomadic invaders.
Estimated millions of workers died building it.
Longest human-made structure on Earth.
The Great Wall was built and rebuilt by multiple Chinese dynasties over centuries.
It stretches over 13,000 miles across northern China's rugged terrain.
Today it stands as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and symbol of Chinese civilization.
The first walls date to the 7th century BC; these were joined together in the Qin dynasty.
The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications in China.
Successive dynasties expanded the wall system; the best-known sections were built by the Ming dynasty.
Other purposes of the Great Wall have included border controls (allowing control of immigration and emigration.

title: The Silk Road
bullets: Trade network linking China to Mediterranean.
Silk spices paper and ideas flowed both ways.
Buddhism spread from India to East Asia.
Marco Polo traveled it in the 13th century.
Declined when sea routes opened in 15th century.
The Silk Road connected merchants, monks, and travelers across thousands of miles.
Paper, gunpowder, and Buddhism spread along its ancient trade routes.
Marco Polo's travels along the Silk Road opened European eyes to Asia's riches.
The Great Silk Road was a network of Asian trade routes active from the second century BCE until the mid-15th century.
Contemporary reports still describe The Silk Road.
Later histories kept returning to The Silk Road.
Surviving photographs still illustrate The Silk Road.

title: Mayan Civilization Collapse
bullets: Peak between 250 and 900 CE in Mesoamerica.
Built pyramids calendars and writing system.
Predicted eclipses with stunning accuracy.
Classic collapse still debated by archaeologists.
Drought warfare and overpopulation likely causes.
The Maya built sophisticated cities with pyramids, observatories, and advanced calendars.
Their writing system was the most developed in the pre-Columbian Americas.
The Classic Maya collapse around 900 CE remains one of archaeology's great mysteries.
The Classic Maya collapse is one of the greatest unsolved mysteries in archaeology.
The Maya civilization was a Mesoamerican civilization that existed from antiquity to the early modern period.
Known by its ancient temples and glyphs, the civilization is also noted for its art, architecture, mathematics, calendar, and astronomical system.
Mayan Civilization Collapse is usually dated to 900 CE.

title: Aztec Empire
bullets: Capital Tenochtitlan built on a lake.
Ruled central Mexico from 1428 to 1521.
Practiced ritual human sacrifice to sun god.
Market of Tlatelolco served 60,000 daily.
Fell to Hernan Cortes and allied tribes.
Tenochtitlan was one of the largest cities in the world when the Spanish arrived.
Aztec engineers built canals, causeways, and floating gardens on a lake.
Spanish conquest and European diseases devastated the Aztec population within decades.
Its people and civil society are historiographically referred to as the Aztecs or the Culhua-Mexica.
The alliance was formed from the victorious factions of a civil war fought between the city of Azcapotzalco and its former tributary provinces.
Despite the initial conception of the empire as an alliance of three self-governed city-states, the capital Tenochtitlan became dominant militarily.
Aztec Empire is usually dated to 1428.

title: Inca Empire
bullets: Largest empire in pre-Columbian Americas.
Capital Cusco high in Andes Mountains.
Built Machu Picchu without iron tools.
Quipu knot system recorded data without writing.
Fell to Francisco Pizarro in 1533.
The Inca ruled an empire of roughly 10 million people without a written language.
They built Machu Picchu and an extensive road network high in the Andes.
Spanish conquistadors captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa and seized their gold.
The Portuguese explorer Aleixo Garcia was the first European to reach the Inca Empire in 1524.
Later, in 1532, the Spanish began the conquest of the Inca Empire, and by 1572 the last Inca state was fully conquered.
The Inca Empire, officially known as the Realm of the Four Parts was the largest empire in pre-Columbian America.
The administrative, political, and military center of the empire was in the city of Cusco.
credit: Pedro Szekely at https://www.flickr.com/photos/pedrosz/ · CC BY-SA 2.0

title: Stonehenge Mystery
bullets: Constructed 3000-2000 BCE on Salisbury Plain.
Some stones dragged 150 miles from Wales.
Aligned with summer and winter solstices.
Purpose debated: temple calendar or burial site.
Built by people without metal tools or wheels.
Some bluestones were transported over 150 miles from Wales.
The monument aligns with the summer and winter solstices.
This was the official name of the site until 1982, when it was renamed "America's Stonehenge", a term coined in a news article in the early 1960s.
It is open to the public for a fee as part of a recreational area which includes snowshoe trails and an alpaca farm.
Some claim that the site has a pre-Columbian European origin, but this is regarded as pseudoarchaeological.
Stonehenge Mystery is usually dated to 2000 BCE.
Another date tied to Stonehenge Mystery is 2000.

title: Rosetta Stone
bullets: Discovered 1799 by French soldiers in Egypt.
Same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphics demotic Greek.
Jean-Francois Champollion cracked code 1822.
Opened 3,000 years of Egyptian history.
Now displayed at British Museum London.
The Rosetta Stone was the key that unlocked the mystery of Egyptian hieroglyphics.
It bears the same decree written in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek scripts.
It was found there in July 1799 by French army officer Pierre-François Bouchard during France's invasion of Egypt.
It was probably moved in late antiquity or during the Mamluk period.
It was the first Ancient Egyptian bilingual text recovered in modern times.
The top and middle texts are in Ancient Egyptian using hieroglyphic and Demotic scripts, respectively, while the bottom is in Ancient Greek.
The decree has only minor differences across the three versions, making the Rosetta Stone key to deciphering the Egyptian scripts.

title: Pompeii Eruption
bullets: Mount Vesuvius erupted in August 79 CE, burying the Roman city of Pompeii.
Volcanic ash preserved bodies, buildings, and graffiti in extraordinary detail.
City of 11,000 buried under 20 feet of ash.
Pliny the Younger witnessed the eruption and left a vivid written account.
Pompeii was rediscovered in 1748, frozen in time beneath the ash.
Mount Vesuvius erupted on August 24, 79 CE, burying Pompeii under volcanic ash.
The ash preserved buildings, artifacts, and haunting body casts for centuries.
Pompeii was rediscovered in 1748 and offers a frozen snapshot of Roman daily life.
The total population of both cities was over 20,000.
The remains of over 1,500 people have been found at Pompeii and Herculaneum.
The event destroyed several Roman towns and settlements in the area.
Pompeii and Herculaneum, obliterated and buried underneath massive pyroclastic surges and ashfall deposits are the most famous examples.

title: Library of Alexandria
bullets: Founded 3rd century BCE in Egypt.
May have held 400,000 scrolls and manuscripts.
Center of ancient science and philosophy.
Destroyed in stages over centuries.
Loss of knowledge still mourned today.
Scholars like Euclid and Archimedes may have studied and worked there.
Its destruction — whether by fire, war, or neglect — remains one of history's greatest losses of knowledge.
It is unknown how many scrolls were housed at any given time, but estimates range from 40,000 to 700,000 at its height.
The Library of Alexandria in Alexandria, Egypt was one of the largest and most significant libraries of the ancient world.
The library was part of a larger research institution called the Mouseion, which was dedicated to the Muses, the nine goddesses of the arts.
A library's collection normally includes printed materials which can be borrowed.
A library is a collection of books, and possibly other materials and media, that is accessible for use by its members and members of allied institutions.

title: Phoenician Alphabet
bullets: Developed circa 1050 BCE in modern Lebanon.
First widely used phonetic alphabet.
Spread via Phoenician maritime trade network.
Ancestor of Greek Latin and Arabic scripts.
Made literacy accessible beyond scribes.
The Phoenician alphabet had just 22 characters, all representing consonant sounds.
Phoenician traders spread their script across the Mediterranean world.
Greek, Latin, Arabic, and Hebrew writing systems all trace roots to Phoenician letters.
It was one of the first alphabets, attested in Canaanite and Aramaic inscriptions found across the Mediterranean basin.
The Phoenician alphabet is an abjad that was used across the Mediterranean civilization of Phoenicia for most of the 1st millennium BC.
The Phoenician alphabet proper was used in Ancient Carthage until the 2nd century BC, when it was used to write the Punic language.
It developed directly from the Proto-Sinaitic script used during the Late Bronze Age, which was derived in turn from Egyptian hieroglyphs.

title: Battle of Marathon
bullets: Athenians defeated Persian invasion 490 BCE.
Outnumbered Greeks used disciplined phalanx.
Legendary runner Pheidippides collapsed after.
His run inspired modern marathon distance.
Saved Western democracy at the brink.
The Athenian victory at Marathon in 490 BCE halted the first Persian invasion of Greece.
The hoplite phalanx formation proved decisive against Persia's larger force.
The legend of Pheidippides running to Athens inspired the modern marathon race distance.
The Battle of Marathon took place in 490 BC during the first Persian invasion of Greece.
It was fought between the citizens of Athens, aided by Plataea, and a Persian force commanded by Datis and Artaphernes.
The battle was the culmination of the first attempt by Persia under King Darius I to subjugate Greece.
The first Persian invasion was a response to Athenian involvement in the Ionian Revolt.

title: Qin Shi Huang Unification
hook: One emperor. One China. BURNED the books.
bullets: First emperor unified China 221 BCE.
Built early Great Wall and terracotta army.
Standardized writing currency and measurements.
Ordered burning of Confucian texts.
Obsessed with immortality and mercury pills.
Qin Shi Huang unified warring Chinese states under one empire in 221 BCE.
He standardized weights, measures, currency, and writing across China.
His tomb complex with the terracotta army reflects his obsession with immortality and power.
The circumference of the inner city is 2.5 km and the outer is 6.3 km.
It is located in modern-day Lintong District in Xi'an, Shaanxi.
The tomb is located in the southwest of the inner city and faces east.
The main tomb chamber housing the coffin and burial artifacts is the core of the architectural complex of the mausoleum.
credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist · Public domain

title: Roman Colosseum
bullets: Completed 80 CE under Emperor Titus.
Hosted gladiator fights and mock sea battles.
Free admission to Roman citizens via bread and circuses.
Estimated 400,000 died in arena over centuries.
Still stands as icon of Roman engineering.
The Colosseum could hold an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators.
Gladiators, wild animals, and mock naval battles entertained Roman crowds.
It remains one of Rome's most iconic landmarks nearly 2,000 years later.
Construction began under the Emperor Vespasian in 72 and was completed in AD 80 under his successor and heir, Titus.
The Colosseum is an elliptical amphitheatre in the centre of the city of Rome, Italy, just east of the Roman Forum.
It is the largest ancient amphitheatre ever built, and is the largest standing amphitheatre in the world.
Further modifications were made during the reign of Domitian.

title: Constantine and Christianity
bullets: Roman emperor from 306 to 337 CE.
Legalized Christianity with Edict of Milan 313.
Founded Constantinople as new capital.
Called First Council of Nicaea 325 CE.
Shifted Rome from pagan to Christian empire.
His conversion helped transform Christianity from persecuted faith to imperial religion.
Constantine ruled the Roman Empire as sole emperor for much of his reign.
During the reign of the Roman emperor Constantine the Great, Christianity began to transition to the dominant religion of the Roman Empire.
Some scholars allege that his main objective was to gain unanimous approval and submission to his authority from all classes.
Whether Constantine sincerely converted to Christianity or remained loyal to paganism is a matter of debate among historians.
Constantine and Christianity is usually dated to 337 CE.
Another date tied to Constantine and Christianity is 325 CE.
credit: Bibliothèque nationale de France · Public domain

title: Attila the Hun
hook: Scourge of God. Rome FEARED him.
bullets: Led Hunnic Empire across Europe 434-453 CE.
Demanded half the Western Roman Empire as tribute.
Invaded Gaul and Italy sacking cities.
Died on wedding night cause disputed.
His death ended major Hunnic threat to Rome.
Attila led the Hunnic Empire across Europe in the mid-5th century CE.
Both the Eastern and Western Roman Empires paid him tribute to avoid invasion.
In 441, he led an invasion of the Eastern Roman Empire, the success of which emboldened him to invade the West.
During his reign, Attila was one of the most feared enemies of the Western and Eastern Roman Empires.
The Huns defeated a second army near Callipolis.
He subsequently invaded Italy, devastating the northern provinces, but was unable to take Rome.
Attila, frequently called Attila the Hun and also known by his nickname The Scourge of God was the ruler of the Huns from 434 until his death in early 453.

title: Boudica's Revolt
hook: She burned London to the GROUND.
bullets: Celtic queen of Iceni tribe in Britain.
Romans flogged her and raped her daughters.
Led army that destroyed Colchester and London.
Killed 70,000 Romans and allies.
Defeated then poisoned herself to avoid capture.
Queen Boudica of the Iceni tribe led a massive uprising against Roman rule in 60-61 CE.
Her forces burned Colchester, London, and St. Albans before facing defeat.
She remains a powerful symbol of resistance and Celtic identity in Britain.
It took place circa AD 60–61 in the Roman province of Britain, and it was led by Boudica, the Queen of the Iceni tribe.
It marked the end of resistance to Roman rule in most of the southern half of Great Britain, a period that lasted until AD 410.
The Boudican revolt was an armed uprising by native Celtic Britons against the Roman Empire during the Roman conquest of Britain.
The location of this battle is not known.

title: Ashoka the Great
bullets: Mauryan emperor of India 268-232 BCE.
Kalinga War deaths horrified him into peace.
Spread Buddhism across Asia via edicts.
Built pillars with earliest readable Indian script.
One of history's greatest rulers of compassion.
The carnage of the Kalinga War horrified him and turned him toward Buddhism.
His edicts on pillars across India promoted nonviolence, tolerance, and moral governance.
A patron of Buddhism, he is credited with an important role in the spread of Buddhism across ancient Asia.
Ashoka's edicts suggest that a few years after the Kalinga War, he was gradually drawn towards Buddhism.
Ashoka, IAST: Aśoka; c. 304 – 232 BCE), most commonly known as Ashoka the Great was Emperor of Magadha from c. 268 BCE until his death.
Ashoka the Great is usually dated to 232 BCE.
Contemporary reports still describe Ashoka the Great.
credit: Photo Dharma from Sadao, Thailand · CC BY 2.0

title: Destruction of Carthage
bullets: Third Punic War ended 146 BCE.
Scipio Aemilianus razed city over 17 days.
Legend says Rome sowed fields with salt.
Removed Rome's greatest Mediterranean rival.
The city was razed and its territory became the Roman province of Africa.
The legend that Rome salted the earth may be myth, but Carthage was utterly erased.
A new Roman commander took over in 148 BC, and fared equally badly.
The siege of Carthage was the main engagement of the Third Punic War fought between Carthage and Rome.
Destruction of Carthage is usually dated to 146 BCE.
Contemporary reports still describe Destruction of Carthage.
Later histories kept returning to Destruction of Carthage.
Surviving photographs still illustrate Destruction of Carthage.
credit: Patrick Verdier, Free On Line Photos · Copyrighted free use

title: Minoan Eruption of Thera
bullets: Massive eruption circa 1600 BCE near Crete.
Devastated advanced Minoan civilization.
Possibly inspired Atlantis legend.
Tsunami hit Crete 100 miles away.
One of largest volcanic events in human history.
A volcano may have erased Atlantis.
The Minoan eruption was a catastrophic volcanic eruption that devastated the Aegean island of Thera circa 1600 BC.
Minoan Eruption of Thera is usually dated to 1600 BCE.
Another date tied to Minoan Eruption of Thera is 1600.
Contemporary reports still describe Minoan Eruption of Thera.
Later histories kept returning to Minoan Eruption of Thera.
Surviving photographs still illustrate Minoan Eruption of Thera.

title: Oracle of Delphi
hook: Kings traveled WEEKS for her words.
bullets: Priestess Pythia delivered prophecies for centuries.
Sitting over volcanic fumes caused trance states.
Consulted before wars and founding cities.
Croesus of Lydia and Alexander the Great visited.
Closed by Christian emperor Theodosius 393 CE.
Empires rose and fell on her riddles.
Pythia was the title of the high priestess of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi in central Greece.
She served as its oracle and was known as the Oracle of Delphi.
Her title was sometimes historically glossed in English as the Pythoness.
During this period, the Delphic Oracle was the most prestigious and authoritative oracle among the Greeks.
The oracle is one of the best-documented religious institutions of the classical Greeks.
The Pythia was established at the latest in the 8th century BC, and was widely credited for her prophecies uttered under divine possession by Apollo.

title: Egyptian Mummification
bullets: Process took 70 days for elite Egyptians.
Brain removed through nose with hooks.
Heart left in body as seat of the soul.
Canopic jars held liver lungs stomach intestines.
Believed necessary for afterlife journey.
Death was just the beginning.
Archaeologists and historians continue to uncover new evidence about Egyptian Mummification.
Ancient sources and modern science together help us reconstruct the world of Egyptian Mummification.
Although specific details changed over time, the preparation of the body, the magic rituals.
Early burials were in simple, shallow oval pits, with a few burial goods.
The ancient Egyptians had an elaborate set of funerary practices that they believed were necessary to ensure their immortality after death.
The ancient burial process evolved over time as old customs were discarded and new ones adopted, but several important elements of the process persisted.

title: Invention of Writing
hook: First words EVER carved in clay.
bullets: Sumerian cuneiform circa 3200 BCE in Mesopotamia.
Started as accounting marks on clay tablets.
Epic of Gilgamesh oldest known literature.
Writing enabled law religion and science.
Most transformative invention in human history.
Before writing there was no history only memory.
The breakthrough behind Invention of Writing built on centuries of experimentation and curiosity.
Technologies born from Invention of Writing still shape daily life in the modern world.
The history of writing traces the development of writing systems and how their use transformed different societies.
Writing allowed the spread of these social modalities and their associated knowledge.
Firstly, writing has some purpose or meaning to it.
True writing, where the content of linguistic utterances can be accurately reconstructed by later readers is a later development.

title: Battle of Cannae
bullets: Hannibal's masterpiece August 216 BCE.
Double envelopment surrounded Roman army.
50,000 Romans killed in single day.
Still studied in military academies worldwide.
Rome refused to surrender after the disaster.
The perfect battle. 50,000 dead.
The outcome of Battle of Cannae reshaped borders, rulers, and the balance of power.
Military academies and historians still analyze the tactics and decisions of Battle of Cannae.
It is regarded as one of the greatest tactical feats in military history and one of the worst defeats in Roman history.
Later historians and military strategists have used Cannae as an exemplary battle of annihilation.
Battle of Cannae is usually dated to 216 BCE.
Contemporary reports still describe Battle of Cannae.

title: Nazca Lines
hook: Giant drawings. Only visible from SKY.
bullets: Created 500 BCE to 500 CE in Peru desert.
Include monkey spider hummingbird and whale.
Lines up to 30 miles long.
Purpose unknown: astronomy rituals or water.
Only fully visible from aircraft altitude.
Who drew a monkey you can only see from space?.
The combined length of all the lines is more than 1,300 km, and the group covers an area of about 50 km2.
The width of the lines varies considerably, but more than half are slightly more than 33 cm wide.
The Nazca lines are a group of geoglyphs made in the soil of the Nazca Desert in southern Peru.
Most lines run straight across the landscape, but there are also figurative designs of animals and plants.
They were made by removing the top layer of reddish-brown ferric oxide–coated pebbles to reveal a yellow-grey subsoil.
There are two major phases of the Nazca lines, Paracas phase, from 400 to 200 BC, and Nazca phase, from 200 BC to 500 AD.

title: Hanging Gardens of Babylon
hook: One of seven wonders. Never FOUND.
bullets: Described by ancient Greek historians.
Said to be tiered gardens in ancient Babylon.
No archaeological evidence confirms location.
May be myth or confused with Assyrian gardens.
One of the great unsolved ancient mysteries.
The wonder that might never have existed.
Archaeologists and historians continue to uncover new evidence about Hanging Gardens of Babylon.
Ancient sources and modern science together help us reconstruct the world of Hanging Gardens of Babylon.
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World listed by Hellenic culture.
It was said to have been built in the ancient city of Babylon, near present-day Hillah, Babil province, in Iraq.
The Hanging Gardens' name is derived from the Greek word κρεμαστός.
This was attested to by the Babylonian priest Berossus, writing in about 290 BC, a description that was later quoted by Josephus.
credit: Unknown author Unknown author · Public domain

title: Peloponnesian War
bullets: 27-year conflict 431-404 BCE.
Athens' empire vs Sparta's land power.
Plague killed Pericles and weakened Athens.
Sparta finally won with Persian gold.
Destroyed golden age of Greek civilization.
Two giants fought until both fell.
With both city-states exhausted from years of fighting, the Peace of Nicias was signed in 421 BC.
The war consists of four related conflicts which have traditionally been combined into one.
The opening phase, called the Ten Years' War or the Archidamian War, began in 431 BC when the Spartan king Archidamus II invaded Attica with his army.
The second phase, the Argive War was a proxy war between Sparta and its Peloponnesian rivals, led by Argos and supported by Athens.
Peloponnesian War is usually dated to 404 BCE.
Contemporary reports still describe Peloponnesian War.
credit: U.S. Army Cartographer, as amended by uploader to correct spelling mist… · Public domain

title: Burning of Persepolis
bullets: Alexander the Great entered Persepolis 330 BCE.
Legend says he burned palace in drunken rage.
Ended Achaemenid Persian Empire.
Treasury looted wealth spread to army.
Symbol of Persian civilization destroyed.
One night of fire. Empire ended.
The earliest remains of Persepolis date back to 515 BC.
Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire.
It is situated in the plains of Marvdasht, encircled by the southern Zagros Mountains, Fars province of Iran.
It is one of the key Iranian cultural heritage sites and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The exact function of Persepolis remains unclear.
The complex was taken by the army of Alexander the Great in 330 BC, and soon after, its wooden parts were completely destroyed by fire.

title: Oracle Bones of China
bullets: Shang Dynasty divination circa 1200 BCE.
Questions carved on ox scapula and turtle shells.
Heat applied until bones cracked for answers.
Earliest confirmed Chinese writing survives.
Asked about war harvests and royal health.
They asked bones about the future.
These questions were carved onto the bone or shell in oracle bone script using a sharp tool.
Intense heat was then applied with a metal rod until the bone or shell cracked due to thermal expansion.
The diviner would then interpret the pattern of cracks and write the prognostication upon the piece as well.
Scapulimancy is the specific term if ox scapulae were used for the divination, plastromancy if turtle plastrons were used.
Diviners would submit questions to deities regarding weather, crop planting, the fortunes of members of the royal family, military endeavors.
Oracle Bones of China is usually dated to 1200 BCE.

title: Black Death
hook: Half of Europe. DEAD in 4 years.
bullets: Pandemic 1347-1351 via fleas on rats.
Killed 30-60 percent of Europe's population.
Flagellants whipped themselves seeking mercy.
Jews falsely blamed and massacred.
Labor shortages eventually weakened feudalism.
Half of Europe gone in four years.
The Black Death was a plague pandemic that occurred in Europe from 1346 to 1353.
The disease was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
The Black Death had far-reaching population, economic, and cultural effects.
There were further outbreaks throughout the Late Middle Ages.
It was one of the most fatal pandemics in human history, leading to the death of up to 50 million people, or 50% of Europe's 14th-century population.
It has been tentatively considered as the second plague pandemic, despite each of these outbreaks being separated by around 500–600 years.
